messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Random item intercepts with mixedmirt
parts:
You shouldn't need to include an ID variable to do this since the mixedmirt() setup already assumes that the individuals are random effect terms (and are treated specially as they are actually complex in that they could be mixed with fixed slope coefficients). This type of setup makes mixedmirt() more/less flexible in some cases. 

Phil


On Wed, Aug 5, 2020 at 12:31 PM Donisha Smith <dsmi...@fiu.edu> wrote:
Hi Phil,

I am currently experimenting with using mixedmirt to derive factor scores from a repeated measures (pre-post) design. According to the package manual, I'm aware that the fixed intercept argument is invalid for polytomous items. I just wanted to receive confirmation that it is possible to model random intercepts for each item, for instance my current syntax is:
----------------------
itemnames = colnames(data[4:25])
mixedmod = mixedmirt(data[4:25],random =~1|ID:itemnames,covdata = data[1:3],1, itemtype = 'graded', SE = T)
-----------------
My dataset is in long format, so, my ID column has duplicate ID's. I am hoping to model random intercepts for each individual item, similar to a crossed design. When I extract the theta values from this model, I notice that this model produced random effects for every clustered individual and their interaction with each item so I am under the impression that I have executed what I wanted; however, I wanted ensure the this is the case.

Thanks!

--

messages.author: c2ee45de0a75c037
messages.subject: Re: Random item intercepts with mixedmirt
parts:
Hi Dr. Phil,

I wanted to thank you for answering my questions (especially the one seeking advice). Your package has also made the analysis process exciting and lead to learn more flexible techniques in item analysis. I noticed that you didn't mention that modeling random intercepts for polytomous data isn't invalid in mirt. I've read articles regarding the RPRI model and most dichotomize their scales to apply a Rasch RPRI model. With the polytomous data, I have to consider threshold shifts and discrimination shifts as opposed to a single intercept shift in a 1PL model. I have looked at older articles
from David Andrich and others debating the validity of the joining adjacent categories and possible violations of invariance. I have conducted my analysis with the original polytomous data. I have also dichotomized my data by categorizing "Not at all" as "0" a non-endorsement and categorized "A little", "A fair amount", "Much", and "Very Much" as endorsements or "1". I lose the gradations among the endorsers; however, I can model longitudinal uniform DIF and random intercepts while constraining the discrimination parameter and derive the pre and post factor scores. From my perspective, in the pre and post conditions, the 4th and 5th categories were rarely endorsed and mirt rescores my data due to skipped categories. Additionally, the graded response model is essentially cumulative/sequential 2pl models. By combining the last four categories, the new difficulty is essentially the proportion of endorsers (originally individuals in four ascending categories). So, if the graded response model is cumulative and derives threshold probabilities from the difference between the probabilities of two adjacent variables, shouldn't a dichotomized scale with the same initial category but fully combined ascending categories be equivalent to its polytomous version?

There's good reason for this of course, and you seem to be aware of the difficulties of modeling a item-probability shifts by way of including only additional intercept parameters per item. It's possible to mimic such a process for polytomous models by way of rating scale models for polytomous response data, but I haven't gotten around to doing this just yet (it's a great topic that I would happily develope, but so far there's been little interest/demand for such a model). It's one of the long todo list items that I'll likely get to at some point in the future.

I have looked at older articles
from David Andrich and others debating the validity of the joining adjacent categories and possible violations of invariance.
Collapsing categories is dangerous and potentially misleading work. Pragmatically speaking, it really only should be done when all else has failed.

I have conducted my analysis with the original polytomous data. I have also dichotomized my data by categorizing "Not at all" as "0" a non-endorsement and categorized "A little", "A fair amount", "Much", and "Very Much" as endorsements or "1". I lose the gradations among the endorsers; however, I can model longitudinal uniform DIF and random intercepts while constraining the discrimination parameter and derive the pre and post factor scores. From my perspective, in the pre and post conditions, the 4th and 5th categories were rarely endorsed and mirt rescores my data due to skipped categories. Additionally, the graded response model is essentially cumulative/sequential 2pl models. By combining the last four categories, the new difficulty is essentially the proportion of endorsers (originally individuals in four ascending categories). So, if the graded response model is cumulative and derives threshold probabilities from the difference between the probabilities of two adjacent variables, shouldn't a dichotomized scale with the same initial category but fully combined ascending categories be equivalent to its polytomous version?

I'm not sure what you are asking here, sorry. 

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Random item intercepts with mixedmirt
parts: Ah, the last paragragh was attempting justify combining categories as my original polytomous scale is graded since many have dichotomized polygamous scales by combining like categories. So, I was attempting to reason out the best way to combine my categories by placing "Not at all" as 0 and the other categories as "1" since they were some level of endorsement. Unfortunately as you mentioned, it is a dangerous practice; however, since I  needed to model sex, time, and sex*time DIF, I believed that dichotomizing and using RPRI model was the best and way to go. I have seen that it is possible to model DIF on factor loadings using MPLUS/LAVAAN; however, I haven't seen DIF modeling for polytomous thresholds in these programs.   Ultimately, I look forward to future MIRT updates!

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Random item intercepts with mixedmirt
parts:
Yes, you are correct that the data provided should be in a 'wide' form; otherwise, the non-independence between the row-wise observations would be violated. This is a more strict structure than one typically finds in multilevel modeling software, but it's adopted in mirt to keep consistent with the rest of the package. 

Phil
